paragraphs: Visual recognition systems often combine nearby feature detector responses into a smaller representation through spatial pooling. The purpose is to retain information useful for recognition while reducing sensitivity to transformations, noise, and clutter. This paper investigates why different pooling choices affect performance, moving beyond comparisons based only on observed recognition results.

The authors identify factors that can obscure the effect of the pooling operation itself. One example is the relationship between how many feature responses enter a spatial pool and the resolution used to extract those features. Changing these quantities together can make it difficult to determine which part of the representation explains a performance difference.

The paper provides a detailed theoretical analysis of max pooling and average pooling, accompanied by extensive empirical comparisons on object recognition tasks. Its contribution is an account of pooling that considers the surrounding feature extraction choices. This matters when interpreting experimental comparisons: an observed advantage may reflect interacting design decisions rather than the pooling rule alone.
icml-2010-a-theoretical-analysis-of-feat.tldr: The paper analyzes max and average pooling while showing how feature extraction choices can confound comparisons between them.

paragraphs: This paper studies classification when examples form a network and connected examples tend to have correlated labels. Such dependencies create an opportunity: information about one example can help classify others through their links. The practical motivation is that obtaining labels can be expensive even when the network connecting the examples is already available.

The authors introduce an active learning algorithm that uses this network structure when learning from selected labeled examples. Its design accounts for the interaction between local classification and collective classification, which uses dependencies across linked instances. The central idea is that the value of labeled data should be considered in the context of the connected prediction problem.

Experiments cover two real-world benchmark domains for collective classification. The authors report very high accuracy with only a small fraction of examples labeled. These results support the usefulness of incorporating links into active learning in the evaluated settings, showing how network information can help make a limited supply of labels more effective.
icml-2010-active-learning-for-networked-.tldr: An active learning algorithm uses network links and collective classification to achieve high accuracy from relatively few labeled examples.

paragraphs: Selecting useful features is especially challenging when a dataset contains many more measured attributes than examples. This paper addresses that setting with a feature selection filter intended to prioritize direct causal relationships with the prediction target. Its motivation is that assessing features through causal considerations may improve which inputs are retained for classification.

The proposed filter, mIMR, stands for min-Interaction Max-Relevance. It uses an information-theoretic notion of interaction to assess groups of inputs. The authors show that this interaction carries information both about a subset's relevance and about its causal relationship with the target. This gives the filter a basis for considering more than predictive relevance alone.

The authors compare mIMR with leading approaches on 25 real microarray datasets and report benefits in classification accuracy and stability. A separate toy causal discovery example demonstrates its effectiveness at identifying direct causal relationships. Together, these findings support incorporating causal aspects into feature assessment, with the classification evidence and the causal discovery illustration addressing distinct parts of the proposal.
icml-2010-causal-filter-selection-in-mic.tldr: The mIMR feature filter uses information-theoretic interactions to prioritize causal relevance and improves accuracy and stability on microarray datasets.

paragraphs: A clustering comparison usually asks which points are grouped together in each result. This paper argues that looking only at those assignments can overlook meaningful differences because it ignores where the points lie in space. The geometry that helped generate the clusters can also matter when deciding how different two clusterings are.

The authors demonstrate failure cases in previous comparison techniques, including an inability to distinguish significant changes in the data being clustered. They then formulate an optimization-based measure that combines group membership information with spatial information. The resulting comparison evaluates both the partition of the data and its geometric organization within a single measure.

The proposed approach eliminates the pathological conditions discussed in the paper and allows comparisons without requiring equal numbers of clusters or identical underlying datasets. The authors also describe it as stable and straightforward to implement. Its broader contribution is to make clustering comparison reflect the data's layout, extending what can be learned from comparing assignments alone.
icml-2010-comparing-clusterings-in-space.tldr: An optimization-based measure compares clusterings using both group assignments and geometry, including across different datasets or cluster counts.

paragraphs: Learning in a repeated game requires an agent to adapt while other participants also influence its results. This paper introduces Convergence with Model Learning and Safety, abbreviated CMLeS, to address several goals together. The algorithm achieves convergence, safety, and targeted optimality against opponents whose behavior depends on a bounded amount of memory.

The main technical contribution concerns that targeted optimality guarantee. CMLeS combines efficient exploration with exploitation, connecting the process of learning about opponents to the process of using that knowledge. The guarantee is expressed in a probably approximately correct, or PAC, sense. It therefore has a probabilistic and approximate form, with memory-bounded adversaries defining the stated target class.

The paper places these results in arbitrary repeated games and also presents a full implementation with empirical evidence of effectiveness. The contribution is the combination of the three learning objectives within one algorithm. Its targeted optimality result specifically retains the memory restriction on adversaries, while the experiments provide evidence about the implemented method's behavior.
icml-2010-convergence-targeted-optimalit.tldr: CMLeS combines convergence and safety with PAC-style targeted optimality against memory-bounded adversaries in repeated games.

paragraphs: Clustering models can assume exchangeability, meaning that rearranging the observations does not change how their grouping is modeled. That assumption can be restrictive when observations have meaningful temporal or spatial relationships. This paper develops distance dependent Chinese restaurant processes, a flexible family of distributions over partitions that permits those relationships to influence clustering.

The authors examine the model's properties and its connections to Bayesian nonparametric mixture models. They also derive a Gibbs sampling method for both observed and mixture settings. The approach supports dependencies between observations in infinite clustering models, allowing time or space to participate in the organization of groups instead of being excluded by exchangeability.

Studies using time-dependent models and three text corpora show that relaxing exchangeability can improve the fit to sequential data. The paper also provides an alternative formulation of the traditional Chinese restaurant process, yielding faster-mixing Gibbs sampling than its original formulation. These are related but distinct benefits: greater modeling flexibility for dependent data and improved sampling behavior for the traditional model.
icml-2010-distance-dependent-chinese-res.tldr: Distance dependent Chinese restaurant processes allow clustering to reflect temporal or spatial dependencies and can improve sequential-data fit.

paragraphs: The paper addresses financial time series through the problem of predicting a stock portfolio's Value at Risk. Its modeling focus is volatility and how it evolves over time. Because the portfolio contains multiple stocks, the proposed approach uses multivariate volatility models, bringing the modeling of several financial series into the same framework.

The authors introduce a class of models called dynamical products of experts. Their defining stated choice is to represent the latent process governing volatilities as an inverse Gamma process. In this formulation, volatility is an underlying evolving quantity within the model. This choice supplies the probabilistic foundation for the proposed treatment of financial time series.

The authors report that their multivariate models significantly outperform the related GARCH and stochastic volatility models in popular use that they compare against. This finding supports the proposed model class relative to those established approaches. The paper's contribution connects a specific representation of evolving latent volatility with improved comparative performance, motivated by the financial task of portfolio risk prediction.
icml-2010-dynamical-products-of-experts-.tldr: Dynamical products of experts model latent volatility with an inverse Gamma process and reportedly outperform related GARCH and stochastic volatility models.

paragraphs: This paper considers learning when the learner can inspect only a few attributes of each training example. The constraint concerns access to information within an example, rather than simply the number of examples available. A motivating case is medical research, where each participant may be willing to undergo only a small number of tests.

The authors develop efficient algorithms for learning a linear predictor under this restriction. Their analysis bounds how many additional examples are sufficient to compensate for incomplete observations. This frames the problem as a tradeoff between the amount of information collected per example and the number of examples used for learning.

Experiments on digit recognition data show high prediction accuracy even when training reveals only four pixels from each image. The result illustrates that severely restricted attribute access can still support useful learning in the evaluated task. Combined with the analysis, it shows how additional examples can help offset limited information per example, without requiring each training observation to be fully visible.
icml-2010-efficient-learning-with-partia.tldr: Efficient linear-learning algorithms compensate for observing few attributes per training example by using a bounded number of additional examples.

paragraphs: FAB-MAP lets a mobile robot recognize previously visited places from camera images, supporting navigation and mapping in large environments without installed infrastructure. A central challenge is visual repetition: different locations can look alike. The paper presents an overview of a probabilistic framework designed to handle place recognition even under that ambiguity.

One technical contribution is learning an approximation to the joint distribution of visual elements. This makes relationships among those elements part of the recognition model, and the authors demonstrate improved place recognition performance. They also investigate approaches for robustness in repetitive environments and introduce an efficient early-exit strategy for testing multiple hypotheses.

The model substantially outperforms standard tf-idf ranking on the place recognition task studied. The authors demonstrate reliable online appearance mapping and loop closure detection over a 1,000-kilometer trajectory, with mean filter updates of 14 milliseconds. These results connect the probabilistic modeling choices to both recognition quality and the speed needed to process observations during a robot's journey.
icml-2010-fab-map-appearance-based-place.tldr: FAB-MAP uses probabilistic visual modeling for reliable camera-based place recognition, demonstrated over 1,000 kilometers with 14-millisecond mean filter updates.

paragraphs: AdaBoost builds a strong classifier by repeatedly selecting simple classifiers and combining their weighted votes. Searching for a suitable classifier at each step can be computationally expensive. This paper reduces that search cost by treating the selection process as a sequence of decisions managed by a multi-armed bandit algorithm.

Each bandit arm represents a subset of the available base classifiers. The bandit learns which subsets are useful and chooses one at each iteration; AdaBoost then searches within that subset. The main change from a previous approach is the use of an adversarial bandit algorithm instead of a stochastic one.

That choice supports a weak-to-strong-learning theorem, establishing that the restricted-search procedure retains a formal boosting guarantee. Benchmark experiments also show that the method can achieve generalization performance similar to standard AdaBoost at roughly one-tenth the computational cost. The contribution therefore combines a substantial observed efficiency gain with theoretical support for the learning principle behind the accelerated procedure.
icml-2010-fast-boosting-using-adversaria.tldr: Adversarial bandits accelerate AdaBoost's classifier search while preserving a formal boosting guarantee and similar benchmark generalization performance.

paragraphs: Graph-based learning requires a way to compare structured objects. This paper introduces the Neighborhood Subgraph Pairwise Distance Kernel, which builds such a comparison from small regions within each graph. The approach represents graph structure through pairs of local neighborhoods and the distances separating them, bringing local patterns and their arrangement into the same representation.

The kernel decomposes a graph into all pairs of small-radius neighborhood subgraphs at increasing distances. To make the comparison efficient, the authors use a fast graph invariant. They show that this produces significant speed improvements when computing the Gram matrix, which contains kernel comparisons between the graphs used for learning.

The method is evaluated across chemoinformatics tasks involving antiviral, anticarcinogenic, and toxicological activity prediction. It achieves competitive performance against several recent graph kernel methods. The findings support the usefulness of combining neighborhood pairs with distance information, while the computational results address the practical expense of assembling the comparisons required by a graph kernel.
icml-2010-fast-neighborhood-subgraph-pai.tldr: A graph kernel compares pairs of local neighborhoods at different distances, speeding Gram matrix computation while remaining competitive on chemoinformatics tasks.

paragraphs: This paper develops a clustering algorithm for data represented by a similarity graph. Its goals are computational efficiency and a provable ability to recover groups. For a graph with n vertices and m edges, the stated running time is O(n log³ n + m log n), giving nearly linear scaling up to logarithmic factors.

The recovery guarantee applies to random graphs generated by a planted partition model. Under that model, the algorithm finds all sufficiently large clusters with high probability. The size qualification is central to the result. The authors provide lower bounds showing that it cannot be improved much, even by an algorithm with unlimited computational resources.

The paper also reports experiments on random graphs whose partitions are generated using Chinese restaurant processes, alongside related algorithms, and applications to clustering DBLP titles. The theoretical contribution links efficient computation to a recovery threshold that is close to an underlying information limit. The experiments extend the investigation to generated partitions and a document-title clustering setting.
icml-2010-finding-planted-partitions-in-.tldr: A nearly linear-time graph clustering algorithm recovers sufficiently large planted clusters with high probability, near a fundamental size threshold.

paragraphs: Learning a kernel from multiple base kernels adds flexibility, but it also raises questions about performance on unseen data. This paper develops generalization bounds for that problem by analyzing the Rademacher complexity of the resulting predictor classes. Its central concern is how the number of available kernels affects the bounds.

For a convex combination of p base kernels with L1 regularization, the bound depends on p through only √log p. The authors show this dependence is tight and substantially better than the previous best bound for the same problem. For nonnegative combinations with L2 regularization, they establish a tight dependence of p to the one-quarter power.

The paper gives related results for other Lq regularizers and discusses how its proof techniques apply to classes of linear functions. Experiments with many kernels support the predicted behavior of generalization error as p changes. The results clarify that expanding the kernel collection can have a much milder complexity cost than earlier bounds suggested, particularly under L1 regularization.
icml-2010-generalization-bounds-for-lear.tldr: Tight generalization bounds show mild dependence on the number of learned base kernels under L1 and L2 regularization.

paragraphs: Multilabel classification normally asks whether each label applies to an example. This paper broadens that setting so that a label can apply to different degrees. Those degrees lie on an ordinal scale: their ordering matters. The motivation is that partial or graded membership is a natural description of some practical classification problems.

The authors formalize this graded multilabel setting and propose two general ways to reduce it to conventional classification problems, including ordinary multilabel classification. These reductions connect the richer output format to established learning tasks. They provide routes for handling ordered membership levels through classification machinery designed for more familiar forms of output.

The paper also considers evaluation, asking how common multilabel performance measures should extend when membership is graded. It presents initial experimental results alongside the problem formulation and reduction strategies. The contribution is therefore a framework for both learning and assessing graded predictions, making the desired degree of label membership an explicit part of the task.
icml-2010-graded-multilabel-classificati.tldr: Graded multilabel classification replaces binary label membership with ordered degrees and provides reductions and evaluation measures for the new setting.

paragraphs: Label ranking asks a learner to produce an ordering of labels for an input. This paper introduces two methods built around the Plackett-Luce model, a probabilistic model for ranking data. Both methods connect the input to a distribution over rankings, but they differ in how they make that distribution depend on the input.

The first method uses instance-based learning and fits probability models that are locally constant. The second estimates a global model in which the Plackett-Luce parameters are functions of the instance. This creates two approaches within the same probabilistic framework: local modeling around instances and a model that describes input dependence globally.

The authors compare both methods with earlier label-ranking approaches and report advantages as well as highly competitive predictive accuracy. Their experimental results are especially favorable when training examples contain incomplete ranking information. This finding makes the methods relevant to learning settings where the available supervision supplies only part of an ordering, while retaining ranking as the prediction task.
icml-2010-label-ranking-methods-based-on.tldr: Two Plackett-Luce label-ranking methods achieve competitive accuracy, particularly when training rankings are incomplete.

paragraphs: This paper studies training data where each input comes with several candidate outputs and no prior indication of which candidate is correct. Such supervision provides useful possibilities without resolving the target for the learner. The authors focus on semantic correspondence, where the goal is to connect an input with an appropriate representation of its meaning.

Their approach solves a related task that has unambiguous supervision using label ranking. They then use task-transfer to explain how and why learning that related task performs well on the original ambiguous problem. The key contribution is this connection between the auxiliary ranking task and the semantic correspondence task the system ultimately needs to solve.

The method is applied to matching natural-language sentences with structured meaning representations. On two benchmarks, it performs competitively with leading methods. These results support the proposed transfer strategy as a practical way to learn from candidate sets, showing that ambiguity in the original training targets can be addressed through a carefully related ranking problem.
icml-2010-label-ranking-under-ambiguous-.tldr: A related, unambiguous label-ranking task enables learning sentence-to-meaning correspondences from ambiguous candidate outputs.

paragraphs: A conditional random field models relationships among output variables given an input. This paper studies how to learn a tree structure for such a model using maximum spanning tree methods. The challenge is to choose which output relationships belong in the tree while taking the conditioning input into account during structure learning.

The authors assign candidate edges weights that use local input information, allowing the approach to scale to large problems. They establish a negative learnability result for a general class of these weights. At the same time, they identify two members of the class with reasonable theoretical foundations: local Conditional Mutual Information and Decomposable Conditional Influence.

Both proposed choices perform very well in practice. On synthetic data and a large-scale fMRI application, the methods outperform existing techniques. The paper therefore pairs a theoretical caution about the broader class with positive evidence for particular members. Its findings support these specific ways of scoring edges without turning their practical success into a general learnability guarantee.
icml-2010-learning-tree-conditional-rand.tldr: Locally informed edge scores enable effective tree CRF structure learning despite a negative learnability result for their broader class.

paragraphs: A collection of text documents can support several meaningful ways of grouping its contents. Producing only one clustering may therefore miss the organization a user wants to see. This paper treats that mismatch as a central limitation of conventional clustering and asks how a system can reveal multiple important dimensions within the same dataset.

The authors propose an algorithm that induces multiple clusterings along those dimensions. It discovers the dimensions without supervision, which is useful when users do not already know the possible ways to organize their data. The aim is to expose different meaningful groupings rather than require the user to specify the desired organizing dimension in advance.

The algorithm's viability is demonstrated on several challenging text classification tasks. These results support the feasibility of discovering multiple clustering dimensions in the evaluated document settings. The contribution expands the purpose of clustering from supplying a single partition to helping users explore how a dataset can be organized, including alternatives they may not have anticipated.
icml-2010-mining-clustering-dimensions-e.tldr: An unsupervised algorithm discovers multiple important ways to cluster text documents, helping users explore alternative organizations of a dataset.

paragraphs: Past learning can shape how people approach a new categorization task. In this paper, transfer means that experience changes prior expectations about which kinds of categories are likely to exist. The research question is whether a statistical learning model can explain this reuse of abstract knowledge across related human learning tasks.

The authors propose the hierarchical Dirichlet process, or HDP, as a model of these transfer effects. They bring a model from machine learning into an empirical study of human categorization. The goal is to compare the model's account of experience-dependent expectations with the transfer behavior that people actually exhibit in controlled settings.

Two laboratory experiments measure the degree of transfer in human learners, and the authors compare the HDP model with participants' performance. They find that it provides a good explanation of the observed transfer. The result supports the HDP as an account of these experimental effects, connecting a statistical model of shared learning with changes in human category expectations.
icml-2010-modeling-transfer-learning-in-.tldr: A hierarchical Dirichlet process model explains transfer effects observed in two laboratory experiments on human categorization.

paragraphs: This paper compares learning algorithms in repeated matrix games, where participants seek to maximize cumulative return over repeated interactions. Earlier experiments had found Q-learning stronger than Nash-based multiagent methods. The authors revisit the empirical comparison through all-against-all tournaments, testing how algorithms perform against a range of other learning strategies.

The first stage finds M-Qubed, S, and bandit-based methods such as UCB strongest on general-sum games. Exp3 performs best on cooperative and zero-sum games in that stage. These results make game type an important part of interpreting the comparison: the experiments identify different leading methods across the evaluated categories.

A second stage examines two modifications: forgetting the distant past and representing recent history through states. Both improve the learning algorithms in the experiments. The final leading group consists of newly enhanced versions of Q-learning and UCB, together with M-Qubed. The findings highlight the empirical value of adapting how a learner retains and represents interaction history.
icml-2010-multi-agent-learning-experimen.tldr: Repeated-game tournaments show that forgetting distant history and encoding recent history improve learners, placing enhanced Q-learning and UCB among the best tested methods.

paragraphs: This paper studies predicting labels on the nodes of a weighted graph, with the unknown labels allowed to be adversarial. It connects the attainable mistake bound to a random spanning tree of the graph. The relevant quantity is the tree's weighted cut size, determined by the unknown labeling of its nodes.

The authors characterize the mistake bound through this quantity up to logarithmic factors and derive a randomized algorithm achieving the optimal mistake bound on any weighted graph. The algorithm samples a spanning tree and then predicts labels on that tree. Its prediction procedure uses constant amortized time and linear space, giving a simple computational form to the theoretical result.

Experiments on real-world datasets show that the method compares favorably with both a global Perceptron approach and local label propagation while running much faster. The contribution links a structural measure of label disagreement to prediction difficulty, then uses a sampled tree to obtain an efficient method with both theoretical and empirical support.
icml-2010-random-spanning-trees-and-the-.tldr: Random spanning trees yield an efficient graph-label prediction algorithm with an optimal mistake bound tied to weighted cut size.

paragraphs: Structured prediction requires outputs with internal organization, which can make complete training annotations expensive to obtain. This paper observes that many such tasks have a simpler companion question: does an input possess a good structure? Answering that binary question can be much easier than supplying the full structured output itself.

For part-of-speech tagging, the companion question asks whether a word sequence has a legitimate corresponding sequence of tags. This supplies indirect supervision about the existence of an acceptable structure. The authors develop a large-margin framework that jointly learns from these binary judgments and from direct annotations of structures, combining the two sources of training information.

Experiments on three natural-language structure learning problems show a significant contribution from the easier-to-obtain indirect supervision. The result supports using companion decision tasks to supplement structured labels. The paper's central contribution is a learning framework that connects inexpensive judgments about structural acceptability with the more detailed prediction task, allowing both forms of evidence to inform training.
icml-2010-structured-output-learning-wit.tldr: A large-margin framework improves structured learning by combining direct annotations with easier binary judgments about whether inputs admit good structures.

paragraphs: Elastic embedding is a dimensionality reduction method that optimizes a nonlinear objective over low-dimensional coordinates. The paper connects this method to both Laplacian eigenmaps and stochastic neighbor embedding, bringing a spectral approach and a nonlinear approach into a shared analysis. It also interprets elastic embedding as learning both point coordinates and affinities between points.

The authors develop a homotopy training method, characterize a critical value of its parameter, and study the resulting behavior. For a fixed homotopy parameter, they provide a globally convergent iterative algorithm that requires no additional user parameters. The parameter-free statement applies to that fixed-parameter iterative procedure, while the homotopy method has its own parameter.

The paper also extends the method to points outside the original training sample. On standard datasets, elastic embedding produces results as good as or better than stochastic neighbor embedding, with greater efficiency and robustness. These findings support the method as a practical embedding approach, while its analysis clarifies relationships between existing families of dimensionality reduction techniques.
icml-2010-the-elastic-embedding-algorith.tldr: Elastic embedding connects spectral and nonlinear dimensionality reduction and matches or improves on SNE results with greater efficiency and robustness.

paragraphs: Link prediction can become difficult when observed relationships are sparse. This paper addresses that problem by learning several heterogeneous link prediction tasks together. Its motivating examples involve predicting links between users and different kinds of items, such as books, movies, and songs, so that related tasks can contribute useful knowledge to one another.

The authors propose a nonparametric Bayesian framework for this collective link prediction problem. It automatically learns similarities between tasks and uses those similarities to adapt knowledge transfer. The framework also introduces separate link functions for different tasks to correct biases and skewed distributions in their link data, accounting for differences between the domains.

Experiments on several real-world datasets show significant improvements over several leading existing methods. These results support jointly modeling heterogeneous relationships as a response to data sparsity. The contribution combines adaptive sharing with explicit treatment of task differences, making the transfer depend on learned inter-task similarity while also accommodating distinctive distributions within each task.
icml-2010-transfer-learning-for-collecti.tldr: A Bayesian framework improves sparse link prediction by learning task similarities and adaptively sharing information across heterogeneous domains.

paragraphs: This paper studies two-stage kernel learning methods based on alignment, a criterion used to guide the choice of a kernel. The authors adopt a different definition of alignment from earlier work and develop theoretical results, learning algorithms, and experiments around it. The central question is how alignment connects kernel selection to useful prediction.

The analysis provides a concentration bound for alignment between kernel matrices and proves that highly aligned kernels admit good predictors for both classification and regression. The authors also show that learning a maximum-alignment kernel can be reduced to a simple quadratic program. This gives an actionable optimization procedure alongside the theoretical motivation for the criterion.

Extensive classification and regression experiments show improvements over uniformly combining kernels and over other leading kernel-learning methods. The paper therefore supports alignment from several directions: its statistical behavior, its relationship to predictor quality, its computational optimization, and its observed performance. The existence result motivates the criterion without asserting that every predictor using a highly aligned kernel must perform well.
icml-2010-two-stage-learning-kernel-algo.tldr: Alignment-based kernel learning gains theoretical support, a quadratic-program formulation, and improved classification and regression results.
